summary: This document specifies using the Constrained Application Protocol (CoAP) to transfer Certificate Management Protocol (CMP) messages. CMP defines how PKI entities interact to create and manage certificates. CoAP is a lightweight HTTP-like protocol used by constrained Internet of Things devices.

plainLanguage.summary: Tiny gadgets need ID cards too, but can't carry heavy paperwork. This lets them talk to the certificate office using light, small messages.

questions: certificate enrollment for iot with coap
how do iot devices get certificates with coap
subtitle: How small IoT devices can talk to a certificate authority using CoAP instead of HTTP.

tldr.problem: The Certificate Management Protocol (CMP) must work over any transport, but constrained devices may prefer the lightweight CoAP over HTTP.
tldr.mechanism: CMP messages are DER encoded and sent as the body of Confirmable CoAP POST requests, with the content-format application/pkixcmp, under the /.well-known/cmp path. Large messages use block-wise transfer.
tldr.outcome: Constrained devices can enrol and manage certificates over CoAP, and a CoAP-to-HTTP proxy lets them reach existing CMP servers unchanged.

today: RFC 9482 is a Proposed Standard published in November 2023. It has not been obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: Why CMP Needs a CoAP Transfer
sections.content:
The Certificate Management Protocol (CMP, RFC 4210) is how PKI entities create and manage certificates. One of its requirements is to be independent of the transport protocol in use.

The Constrained Application Protocol (CoAP, RFC 7252) is a client-server protocol like HTTP, designed for constrained devices on constrained networks. Its recommended transport is UDP. This document specifies CoAP over UDP as a transport for CMP version 2, CMP version 3 (RFC 9480) and the Lightweight CMP Profile (RFC 9483), and follows the HTTP transfer rules of RFC 6712 in general.

End entities (EEs) may be constrained devices, while registration authorities (RAs) and certification authorities (CAs) are usually not and can support both CoAP and HTTP.
sections.plainLanguage: Getting an ID card from the office normally means a lot of paperwork. Tiny gadgets cannot carry that, so this gives them a lighter way to ask.

sections.title: URI Format and Discovery
sections.content:
CoAP endpoints MUST support the path prefix /.well-known/ with the registered name cmp. Optional path segments may follow. The segment p plus a label can pick a specific CA or certificate profile, and a further segment can name a PKI operation, as in the Lightweight CMP Profile.

A device can be configured with just the scheme (coap: or coaps:) and the authority. If no port is given, the defaults are 5683 for coap: and 5684 for coaps:.

Where a Local RA or CA is deployed, devices can optionally use CoAP service discovery. Endpoints that support it MUST also support resource discovery in CoRE Link Format, and the link MUST include the ct attribute with the value application/pkixcmp.
sections.plainLanguage: Every certificate office gets a standard street address, so a gadget knows where to knock. It can also shout out and ask who is nearby.

sections.title: Sending CMP Messages in CoAP Requests
sections.content:
CMP PKIMessages MUST be DER encoded and sent as the body of a CoAP POST request. The client MUST mark each request as a Confirmable message, and the content-format application/pkixcmp MUST be used.

On success the RA or CA MUST return a 2.xx response. Otherwise it MUST return an appropriate 4.xx (client error) or 5.xx (server error) code. The server may send a piggybacked response, or a separate response if processing takes some time.

CMP messages over CoAP MUST NOT use a multicast destination address.
sections.plainLanguage: The gadget puts its request in an envelope marked 'please confirm you got this'. The office answers with a code that says whether it worked.

sections.title: Block-Wise Transfer for Large Messages
sections.content:
A PKIMessage has a header, body, protection and extraCerts, some of which can be large, so a message can be much bigger than the MTU of the device's outgoing interface. EEs, RAs and CAs MUST use the block-wise transfer mode (RFC 7959) for such messages instead of relying on IP fragmentation.

If a CoAP-to-HTTP proxy sits in the path and the server supports it, the proxy MUST use chunked transfer encoding (RFC 9112) on the HTTP side and try to reduce the number of packets by choosing an optimal chunk length.
sections.plainLanguage: If a parcel is too big for the mail slot, you send it in several small pieces instead of squashing it through.

sections.title: Announcements and the Proxy
sections.content:
A CMP server may publish announcements: CA Key Update (15), Certificate (16), Revocation (17) and CRL (18). An EE MAY use the CoAP Observe Option (RFC 7641) to register by sending a GET to the server URI suffixed with /ann. If the server cannot add the client as an observer, it can omit the Observe Option in its response, and the client MAY try again later. An EE SHOULD periodically reregister. As an alternative, an EE MAY poll with the PKI Information Request message or use support messages from RFC 9483.

Because the CMP payload is the same over CoAP and HTTP, a CoAP-to-HTTP cross-protocol proxy can be built on Section 10 of RFC 7252. It can sit near the EEs or near the RA or CA, and it MUST act as a reverse proxy that only permits connections to a limited set of preconfigured servers. Routing is out of scope, but the RFC suggests using the Uri-Path option, separate hostnames with the Uri-Host option, or Server Name Indication for coaps://.
sections.plainLanguage: A gadget can sign up for news from the certificate office, or just ask now and then. A helper at the door can translate between the gadget's light language and the office's usual one.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
If PKIProtection is used, the PKIHeader and PKIBody are cryptographically protected against modification, so UDP can be used without weakening CMP. CMP itself does not give confidentiality. If it is wanted, CoAP over DTLS (RFC 9147) SHOULD be used, and DTLS associations SHOULD be kept alive and reused to amortise overhead on constrained devices.

Observe is best-effort, so an EE might miss announcements. For time-critical changes such as CRL updates it may use the polling alternative. Implementations SHOULD use the available datagram size and avoid small datagrams carrying partial PKIMessage data.

A CoAP-to-HTTP proxy can help protect PKI entities by checking ASN.1 syntax and PKIMessage protection, which can mitigate denial-of-service, replay and resource-exhaustion attacks. It may itself be exposed to resource exhaustion because it buffers messages. The RFC suggests short timers for buffered messages and rate limiting clients, and says proper role-based access control should be in place.
sections.plainLanguage: The messages carry their own lock, but nobody hides what is inside unless you add a secret tunnel. The helper at the door can also turn away troublemakers.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
IANA registered the content-format application/pkixcmp (ID 259) in the CoAP Content-Formats registry. It also registered the new path segment ann in the CMP Well-Known URI Path Segments registry, for registering for announcement messages.

This document was also added as a reference for the cmp entry in the Well-Known URIs registry and for the p entry in the CMP Well-Known URI Path Segments registry.
sections.plainLanguage: The official list of names was updated so that everyone uses the same label for these messages.
